data.text/markdown:
3D metric maps from a point cloud

This notebook uses the MRPT Python wheel (pip install mrpt3) to build five different 3D map representations from the same simulated 3D LiDAR scan, and compares them. All maps live in mrpt.maps and share the CMetricMap interface:
  • CSimplePointsMap: the raw point cloud.
  • CVoxelMap: a sparse voxel map with occupancy probabilities.
  • COctoMap: an octree of occupancy probabilities (the OctoMap library).
  • COccupancyGridMap3D: a dense 3D occupancy grid.
  • CHeightGridMap2D: a 2.5D elevation map (one height per cell).
The scan is wrapped in a CObservationPointCloud (mrpt.maps) and inserted into every map with the same call, insertObservation(), from a CPose3D sensor pose (mrpt.poses). Move the sliders: change the map resolution, pick which map to see in 3D, and aim a probe ray to query the maps.

1. A simulated 3D LiDAR scan

The world is a walled yard (16 x 12 m) with a table, a cabinet, stacked crates, a ball and a tree. A 32-ring rotating LiDAR, 1.3 m above the ground, casts 32,768 rays (elevations from -30° to +10°) against it. Ray casting is done with NumPy, and the resulting points (in the sensor frame) go into a CSimplePointsMap.
Simulated scan: 31,584 points in a CObservationPointCloud.

2. Five map representations

  • Point cloud: keeps every measurement, no resolution, no free space.
  • Occupancy maps (CVoxelMap, COctoMap, COccupancyGridMap3D): each ray marks the voxels it crosses as free and its end voxel as occupied, fusing evidence as log-odds probabilities. Voxels never crossed by a ray stay unknown. They differ in how voxels are stored: a sparse block grid, an octree, or a dense array that allocates every voxel of the bounding box.
  • Height map (CHeightGridMap2D): stores one mean height per (x, y) cell. Compact and good for terrain, but it cannot represent overhangs (the space under the table or the tree crown) and averages vertical surfaces.
The occupancy maps have no bulk export in Python, except CVoxelMap.getOccupiedVoxels(): for the other two, the 3D view queries their occupancy at the voxels that contain a measured point.

data.text/html: Parameters

data.text/markdown:
Map class What is stored Size at 0.20 m Insertion time
CSimplePointsMap x, y, z of each point (float32) 31,584 points (0.38 MB) 0.5 ms
CVoxelMap blocks of observed voxels only (sparse) 7,686 occupied voxels 8.3 ms
COctoMap octree nodes (free, occupied, inner) 63,570 nodes, 9,835 occupied voxels 30.3 ms
COccupancyGridMap3D every voxel of the box (1 byte each) 84 x 64 x 16 = 86,016 voxels (0.09 MB), 8,174 occupied 3.5 ms
CHeightGridMap2D one height per (x, y) cell 84 x 64 = 5,376 cells, 2,594 observed 1.2 ms
The dense grid grows with the volume of its bounding box (x8 when halving the voxel size), observed or not, while the sparse maps only store what the rays touched. Ray tracing makes the occupancy maps slower to build than a point cloud, in exchange for knowing which space is free.

3. Querying the maps along a ray

The red probe ray starts at the sensor. Below, the occupancy maps are queried along it (getPointOccupancy(), getFreenessByPos()). By default it hits the stacked crates: the probability is low in free space, high at the crate, and unknown behind it (the dense grid cannot tell unknown from p = 0.5). COctoMap updates each voxel once per scan (hits win), hence its flat 0.4 / 0.7 values, while the other two maps fuse every ray. The bottom plot compares the ray height with the height map (getHeight()) along the same path. Each cell holds the mean height of its points, so the crates (1.6 m tall) look lower than they are, and their vertical front face becomes a ramp.

Run it on your computer (Linux, Python 3.11 to 3.14): 
uvx marimo edit --sandbox https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MRPT/mrpt-notebooks/main/notebooks/point_cloud_maps.py
More MRPT Python examples: mrpt_examples_py.
